objectives.text: Keep Sadyr Japarov in power through the presidential election of 27 January 2027. His former partner Kamchybek Tashiev was sacked on 10 February 2026 and convicted in July 2026 of plotting to seize power by force. In February 2026 the Constitutional Court ruled that Japarov's current mandate counts as his first term, so he can run again.

objectives.text: Keep the Russian security umbrella and the labour market open at the same time: CSTO membership with the Kant air base near Bishkek, and the wages of migrants who work mostly in Russia. Bishkek wants the protection without Moscow's political control.

means.text: Multi-vector diplomacy: CSTO and EAEU membership with Russia, the railway and Chinese financing, Turkic bodies with Turkey, and a Washington channel (C5+1 summit, November 2025) that Bishkek presents as trade, fintech and visas rather than minerals. Military: the CSTO framework: Russian forces at the Kant air base, which Moscow says is enough for the southern flank with no expansion needed; Russian personnel took part in the Rubezh-2025 exercise. Turkish drones (TB2 bought in 2021, more ordered after the 2022 clashes with Tajikistan) add a second air arm.

means.text: Control of the press: Kloop, whose liquidation a court ordered in February 2024 (it kept working under another entity), had its current and former staff detained in May 2025 in the so-called Kempir-Abad case. Two former employees were jailed for five years in September 2025. Critics call the charges baseless; the government says closing Kloop does not jeopardise press freedom.

means.text: Gold: the Kumtor mine, the largest in Central Asia, came under state control in May 2021 and passed to 100 per cent Kyrgyz ownership in April 2022 through a settlement with Centerra. It is the country's main private employer and taxpayer.

constraints.text: Russia is the labour market and the money. Remittances were about a quarter of GDP in 2024 (24 to 25 per cent in reporting citing the World Bank), and Russia supplied 94 per cent of inflows in January-May 2025. Russian rules since 2024 (90-day stays, fingerprinting, expulsion of about 157,000 irregular migrants in 2024) cut the official count of Kyrgyz workers from about 650,000 to about 350,000, though unofficial estimates are higher.

constraints.text: A small economy with Kremlin dependence: the economy depends on Russia directly and through Kazakhstan, which limits what Bishkek can refuse in Moscow. The CSTO and the Kant base are the security side of the same dependence.

The intergovernmental agreement was still being prepared in 2025-26 and the cost is disputed ($4.2bn to $5bn), so the water lever is not yet in Bishkek's hands.

grand_strategy.reading: Kyrgyzstan is a small, landlocked state whose regime has concentrated power around Japarov since he sacked Tashiev in February 2026, ahead of a presidential election on 27 January 2027, after a 2025 crackdown on the independent press. Its security and its labour market both run through Russia (CSTO, Kant, remittances), while China (railway and financing), Uzbekistan and Tajikistan (border treaties of 2023 and 2025) and the United States (trade and visas) offer room to balance. Its levers are gold, transit and water; its binding constraint is Moscow.

stances.note: CSTO member (treaty alliance, with the Kant air base under the CSTO framework) and EAEU member. Bond is affinity, not kin: Russian language and Soviet legacy, but a multi-vector state that keeps its own elite and its own trade with China. The labour and remittance dependence (about a quarter of GDP) is a constraint on the posture, not a reason to downgrade it. The 2024-25 migrant crackdown is friction in the labour channel, not a change of alignment.

stances.note: Transactional partner with the largest external financing and the railway. Bishkek ratified the Central Asia-China treaty on good-neighbourliness (September 2025) and the railway works began on 27 December 2024. The 1996 and 1999 border agreements that would have ceded about 125,000 hectares sparked a parliamentary revolt in 2025, a reminder that the bond is interest, not kinship. Its grade follows structure, not rhetoric: it is not an ally.

stances_toward.note: Border clashes in 2021 and 2022 left scores dead and thousands displaced (sources differ on the scale; they were a series of clashes rather than one war). The Treaty on the Kyrgyz-Tajik State Border, signed in Bishkek on 13 Mar 2025 with 16 documents during Rahmon's visit, ratified by Kyrgyzstan in June-July 2025, and the first border pillars installed on 14 Jul 2025, make Bishkek a partner now. No alignment treaty; Tajikistan keeps its CSTO and Russian ties. Bond - grievance: the 2021-22 clashes, the closed frontier and the Vorukh enclave. Trend warming since the March 2025 treaty; if the demarcation stalls, the grade should be read again.
